forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Stoke-on-Trent repays £20m of LOBO loans at par after lender reset rates, borrowing from PWLB instead
news_drafts.lead:
Stoke-on-Trent City Council repaid two £10m loans in April 2026 after the bank that lent the money moved to change the interest rate, according to the first-quarter treasury management report (how a council borrows, invests spare cash and manages the risks of both) to 30 June 2026. The report goes to the Audit and Standards Committee.

The loans were LOBO loans: bank loans where, on set dates, the lender may propose a higher interest rate and the council may then repay the loan in full instead of accepting it. Together they totalled £20m, carried a 3.84% interest rate and were not due to end until 5 April 2066. The report says the lender exercised its option to change the rates, and "rather than accept the revised rates, the Council used its contractual option to repay the £20.000m principal". It repaid at par, meaning the amount originally borrowed.

The council replaced the money with shorter-life borrowing from the Public Works Loan Board (PWLB), the government's lending arm for councils, run by the Treasury. That was taken at an average rate of 5.00%, higher than the 3.84% on the old loans. The change removes about 40 years during which a lender could alter the interest rate, and simplifies the council's debt, the report says.
news_drafts.paper_title: Treasury Management 2026/27 Q1 (first quarter to 30 June 2026)

findings.headline: Risk register lists introduction of a new financial system (ERP) in 2026-27, with risks around delay, testing and training.
findings.detail: The paper's ERP risk lists delay necessitating alternative system provision, failure to test adequately, results not delivered and staff not trained. The control list for the financial management risk includes the new system as a control.
findings.matters: Finance system go-lives carry close and reporting risk, and other finance teams planning similar changes will compare the risks listed.
findings.quote: Development and introduction of new financial system in 2026-27 (ERP).

findings.headline: Council is strengthening its contingent liabilities process through a central register, clearer ownership and standard probability and value assessments.
findings.detail: The paper says the strengthened process will improve in-year visibility of changes and support earlier consideration of budget, reserve, cash-flow and MTFS implications. It also states contingent liabilities are reviewed quarterly as part of budget monitoring.
findings.matters: A central register with standard assessments is a governance change other councils may consider when tightening their own contingent liability reporting.
findings.quote: the process will be strengthened through a central register, clearer ownership, standard probability and value assessments, documented quarterly review and defined escalation requirements.

findings.headline: Risk 01, "failure to achieve 2026/27 savings to balance the budget", is scored 5:5 (25) Very High with a target of 4:3 (12) High at Qtr 2
findings.detail: The Qtr 2 control list adds monthly monitoring of savings delivery, recovery actions and expenditure controls. The annex does not give a figure for savings delivered to date.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council will compare how the risk is scored and controlled against their own savings delivery tracking.
findings.quote: FAILURE TO ACHIEVE PROPOSED SAVINGS TO BALANCE THE BUDGET IN 2026/27

findings.headline: Transfer of working-age claimants to Universal Credit was completed by March 2026; migration of a small number of pensioners on Pension Credit is due in October 2026.
findings.detail: The paper says a timeline for the remaining pensioners has not yet been announced, but it is expected that all pensioners will eventually transfer from Housing Benefit to Universal Credit, which will result in less Housing Benefit funding.
findings.matters: Each stage of Universal Credit migration reduces Housing Benefit subsidy flows, which finance directors across councils need to model.
findings.quote: The transfer of Working Age claimants to Universal Credit was completed by March 2026.

findings.headline: The 2025/26 IAS 19 review finds the Pension Fund in a strong funded position, with the accounting surplus restricted under IFRIC 14.
findings.detail: The paper says the review has not identified an immediate funding or affordability concern. It adds that the council remains exposed to investment market, inflation, interest rate, longevity and membership movements, which could become material over the medium to long term.
findings.matters: A surplus that cannot be recognised as an asset under IFRIC 14 affects how any council reports its pension position, which other finance directors will compare.
findings.quote: The Pension Fund is in a strong funded position, although the accounting surplus is fully restricted under IFRIC 14 and cannot currently be recognised as an asset.

daily_post.headline: Four high-risk recommendations from 2024 Residential Care Homes audit remain unimplemented as of September 2026.
daily_post.lead: Audit recommendations identify required control improvements. Unimplemented high-risk recommendations in regulated adult social care mean expected controls remain absent. A gap of up to two years between audit issuance and outstanding implementation…
